pecheur.intro: Joins two ropes securely, or closes a cord into a loop (for a Prusik). Doesn't come undone by itself.
etapes: Lay the two ends side by side, pointing in opposite directions.
With the first end, make two turns around both ropes working back towards you, then pass it through these two turns.
Do the same with the second end, in the other direction.
Pull on the two ropes: the two knots slide together and lock against each other.
attention: Very hard to untie after a heavy load.
pecheur.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska; US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

prusik.intro: A loop of cord that slides by hand along a rope and locks under load. For tensioning a tarp on a ridgeline or climbing up a rope.
etapes: Take a cord thinner than the main rope, closed into a loop (double fisherman's knot).
Pass the loop behind the main rope.
Pass the loop through itself around the rope, three times.
Dress the turns neatly parallel and tighten: push the knot to move it, pull the loop to lock it.
attention: The thinner the cord compared with the rope, the harder it grips.
prusik.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska; US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

bois.intro: For dragging a log or carrying a bundle of wood. Holds by tension and comes undone in one move.
etapes: Pass the rope around the log or bundle.
Make a half hitch around the standing part.
Wrap the working end three times around itself, along the loop.
Pull to tighten. To drag a long log, add a half hitch further towards the end.
bois.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska; US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

constricteur.intro: The tightest-gripping knot: closing a bag, binding a bundle, making an emergency whipping on a pole.
etapes: Make one turn around the object.
Cross over and make a second turn, like a clove hitch.
Tuck the working end under the X crossing, so it comes out between the two strands.
Pull both ends hard to tighten.
attention: Almost impossible to untie once tight: plan to cut it.
constricteur.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska; US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

brelagecarre.intro: Joins two poles crosswise for a shelter frame, a table or a drying rack.
etapes: Cross the two poles at right angles.
Tie a clove hitch on the upright pole, just below the crosspiece.
Make 3 to 4 turns: over the crosspiece, behind the upright, over the crosspiece on the other side, behind the upright.
Make 2 to 3 frapping turns between the two poles, around the previous turns.
Finish with a clove hitch on the crosspiece.
attention: Only with dead wood, and dismantle it before leaving.
brelagecarre.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska; US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

brelagetrepied.intro: Joins two or three poles to make a tripod (hanging a pot, raising a ridgepole).
etapes: Lay the poles side by side, ends aligned.
Tie a clove hitch on an outer pole.
Make 8 to 10 loose turns around all the poles.
Make 2 frapping turns between each pole.
Finish with a clove hitch, then spread the legs: the turns tighten by themselves.
brelagetrepied.source: Standard knotting methods, written for Bivaska; US Army survival manual FM 21-76 / FM 3-05.70 (public domain)

ps_saignement.intro: Bleeding can almost always be controlled by firm direct pressure.
etapes: Protect your hands if possible (gloves, plastic bag).
Press hard and without letting go directly on the wound with a clean cloth, for at least 10 minutes.
If the cloth fills with blood, don't remove it: add another on top and keep pressing.
Lay the casualty down, cover them, call 112 if the bleeding doesn't stop or is heavy.
Small wound: rinse with drinking water, disinfect, cover with a plaster.
attention: A tourniquet is only a last resort, on a limb, when direct pressure isn't enough, noting the time it was applied.
isole: Press hard and without letting go for at least 10 minutes, timed: continuous pressure is what stops the bleeding.
If it starts again: press again for 20 minutes, fingers right on the bleeding spot, through a clean cloth.
Once it has stopped: make a pressure dressing (folded cloth on the wound, bandage or scarf tied firmly on top) and check that the fingers or toes stay pink and warm.
A limb that spurts blood or won't stop despite pressure: apply a tourniquet (Improvised tourniquet sheet).
Once the bleeding is under control: clean the wound with plenty of drinking water (Treating a wound sheet) and check it every day.
Give fluids, keep warm and rested: blood loss weakens and chills you.
alerte: Blood spurts or soaks everything within minutes
Wound to the neck, chest or belly
Pallor, cold sweats, fast pulse: shock
ps_saignement.source: Public first-aid guidance (Red Cross, ULB); Belgian Poison Centre; manual FM 4-25.11 (public domain)

ps_ampoule.intro: The hiker's number one enemy. Better to treat the hot spot before it blisters.
etapes: As soon as an area gets hot, stop and protect it (second-skin plaster, tape).
Closed blister: don't pop it, protect it with a special plaster or a foam ring around it.
Open blister: clean it, don't tear off the skin, cover with a clean dressing.
Change wet socks: damp encourages blisters.
attention: Spreading redness, pus or fever: sign of infection, see a doctor.
isole: Stop as soon as an area gets hot and protect it before it opens.
A very tight blister that stops you walking: pierce it at the edge with a disinfected needle (flame then alcohol), press gently, keep the skin in place.
Cover with a dressing and pad around it (foam, folded cloth) so the shoe no longer presses on it.
At every break, dry and air your feet. At night, sleep in dry socks.
Redo the dressing every day, rinsing with drinking water.
alerte: Spreading redness or a red streak up the leg
Pus, heat, fever
ps_ampoule.source: Public first-aid guidance (Red Cross, ULB); Belgian Poison Centre; manual FM 4-25.11 (public domain)

ps_entorse.intro: A misstep on a wet path happens quickly. What matters: knowing whether you can still walk.
etapes: Stop and rest the ankle.
Cool it for 20 minutes with cold water or a cold pack wrapped in cloth (never directly on the skin).
Raise the leg.
If you can't take 4 steps, or if the pain is sharp on the bone: don't force it, call for help.
attention: Don't remove the shoe if the foot swells a lot and you still have to walk to an access point.
isole: Cool it for 20 minutes in the cold water of a stream or with a wet cloth, several times a day, and raise the leg when resting.
To set off again: keep the shoe on, lace it tight, or make a figure-eight bandage around the ankle with a bandage or scarf.
Make a walking stick from a strong branch at hip height, held on the side opposite the injured ankle.
Lighten the pack, shorten the stages and take the flattest path, even if it is longer.
Can't put the foot down: immobilise it like a fracture (Splint sheet), settle somewhere sheltered and signal rather than forcing it.
alerte: Unable to take 4 steps
Deformity or bone very painful to touch
Foot cold, pale or numb
ps_entorse.source: Public first-aid guidance (Red Cross, ULB); Belgian Poison Centre; manual FM 4-25.11 (public domain)

ps_brulure.intro: Vital reflex: cool for a long time with lukewarm water.
etapes: Cool immediately under lukewarm water for 15 to 20 minutes (30 minutes for a chemical).
Remove rings and clothing that are not stuck to the skin.
Don't burst blisters, don't apply anything (no butter, toothpaste or ice).
Cover with a clean cloth or cling film.
Call 112 if the burn is bigger than the casualty's palm, or affects the face, hands, joints or genitals.
attention: Clothes on fire: stop the person from running, make them roll on the ground or smother the flames with a blanket.
isole: Cool for 20 minutes with water from the stream or the bottle. It is still useful if you couldn't do it straight away.
Cool the burn, not the person: keep the rest of the body covered and warm.
Don't burst blisters. Cover with a clean, dry dressing or cling film.
Redo the dressing once a day, rinsing gently with drinking water.
Give plenty to drink: an extensive burn makes the body lose water.
alerte: Burn bigger than 10 of the casualty's palms: risk of shock
Face, neck, hoarse voice, cough, soot in the nose: the airway may swell
White, leathery or painless burn: deep burn
ps_brulure.source: Public first-aid guidance (Red Cross, ULB); Belgian Poison Centre; manual FM 4-25.11 (public domain)

ps_intox.intro: Poison centres answer 24/7: Belgium 070 245 245, Luxembourg 8002 5500, Switzerland 145, France: your regional poison centre or 15. Elsewhere: 112.
etapes: Call the poison centre (numbers above), or 112 if the person has trouble breathing, loses consciousness or has seizures.
Keep the leftovers: the plant, raw or cooked mushrooms, even peelings, for identification.
Note the time of the meal, the amount and the time of the first symptoms.
Don't make them vomit and don't give anything to drink without medical advice.
attention: Mushrooms: symptoms that appear 6 hours or more after the meal often signal serious poisoning (liver, kidneys), even if the person feels better afterwards.
isole: Stop eating, keep all the leftovers (even peelings) and note the time of the meal.
Don't make them vomit.
If the person is conscious and not vomiting: small regular sips of water to make up for losses.
Note the time of each symptom (nausea, diarrhoea, vision problems, sweating, confusion).
Unconscious and breathing: recovery position, and watch them constantly.
Mushrooms and first symptoms 6 hours or more after the meal: getting out or getting found becomes the absolute priority, even if the person seems better.
alerte: Drowsiness, confusion, seizures
Symptoms appearing 6 h or more after a mushroom meal
Skin or eyes turning yellow
ps_intox.source: Public first-aid guidance (Red Cross, ULB); Belgian Poison Centre; manual FM 4-25.11 (public domain)

ps_morsure.intro: Adder bites are very rare in Belgium, but the right actions are simple.
etapes: Stay calm and lie down: agitation speeds up the spread of venom.
Immobilise the bitten limb, remove rings, watch and bracelets.
Disinfect the bite.
Call 112.
attention: Never suck, aspirate or cut the bite, and never apply a tourniquet.
isole: Stay calm, sit or lie down: most adder bites in Europe are not serious, but you must limit effort.
Immediately remove rings, watch, bracelet, and the shoe if it's the foot, before it swells.
Immobilise the limb with a splint (Splint sheet), without tightening.
Every hour, mark the edge of the swelling with a pen and the time: you'll see whether it's spreading.
Drink water, don't eat, don't drink alcohol.
Don't walk if you can avoid it: signal for help. If you must leave alone, walk slowly and take breaks.
alerte: Swelling goes past the knee or elbow
Vomiting, feeling faint, sweating, swelling of the face
Bleeding from the gums or nose
ps_morsure.source: Public first-aid guidance (Red Cross, ULB); Belgian Poison Centre; manual FM 4-25.11 (public domain)

ps_piqure.intro: Painful but harmless… unless there's an allergy or a sting in the mouth.
etapes: Bee: remove the sting by scraping it with a fingernail or a card, without squeezing the venom sac.
Cool with cold water to limit swelling.
Watch the person for 30 minutes.
Call 112 if the face or throat swells, if there is difficulty breathing, feeling faint or multiple stings. If the person has an adrenaline pen, help them use it.
attention: Sting in the mouth: suck ice or cold water and call 112 if it swells.
isole: Bee: scrape out the sting with a fingernail or card. Cool with cold water.
Watch the person for at least an hour.
Itchy local swelling: antihistamine from the kit if you have one.
Known allergy with an adrenaline pen: inject into the side of the thigh, even through trousers. If there's no improvement after 5 to 15 minutes and you have a second pen, use it.
Difficulty breathing: keep them sitting, leaning forward. Feeling faint: lying down, legs raised.
alerte: Swelling of the face, lips or throat
Wheezing, change in voice
Red blotches all over the body, feeling faint
Sting in the mouth
ps_piqure.source: Public first-aid guidance (Red Cross, ULB); Belgian Poison Centre; manual FM 4-25.11 (public domain)

ps_tique.intro: Check every bivouac evening: armpits, groin, behind the knees, scalp.
etapes: Remove the tick as early as possible with a tick remover, twisting without pulling.
Don't put anything on it first (no ether, alcohol or oil).
Disinfect and note the date and place of the bite.
Watch the area for a month: a redness spreading in a ring or fever means seeing a doctor.
isole: Inspect the whole body every evening and morning: armpits, groin, behind the knees, navel, scalp.
Remove each tick with the tick remover, twisting without pulling. Without one: fine tweezers gripped close to the skin, pulling slowly and straight.
Disinfect and note the date and place in the app's notebook.
Back home, watch the area for a month.
alerte: Spreading ring-shaped redness (show a doctor when you get back)
Fever, great tiredness, joint pain in the following weeks
ps_tique.source: Public first-aid guidance (Red Cross, ULB); Belgian Poison Centre; manual FM 4-25.11 (public domain)

feu_appentis.intro: Ideal in wind or light rain: an angled stick protects the tinder and guides the flame.
etapes: Push a green stick into the ground, angled at about 30°, the tip pointing into the wind.
Tuck a good handful of tinder right at the back, under the stick.
Lean kindling against the stick, on both sides, leaving air gaps.
Light the tinder on the wind side, then add kindling as it catches.
feu_appentis.source: US Army survival manual FM 3-05.70 (public domain), rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

feu_croix.intro: A small cross-shaped trench under the tinder creates a draught: useful when there is no wind.
etapes: Mark a cross about 30 cm across in the ground and dig it 7 to 8 cm deep.
Put a big ball of tinder in the centre of the cross.
Build a small pyramid of kindling on top.
Light it: air flows through the trenches and feeds the flame from below.
attention: Fill in the trenches when you leave, once the ashes are cold.
feu_croix.source: US Army survival manual FM 3-05.70 (public domain), rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

feu_pyramide.intro: A fire that burns slowly from the top down, without needing attention during the night.
etapes: Lay two parallel logs on the ground.
Cover them with a tight layer of logs laid across.
Add 3 or 4 layers, each thinner than the last and crossed at right angles.
Light a small starter fire (teepee) at the very top of the pyramid.
The fire burns down layer by layer and gives heat for hours.
attention: Even a “self-tending” fire must never be left unattended near a shelter or in a dry forest.
feu_pyramide.source: US Army survival manual FM 3-05.70 (public domain), rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

feu_dakota.intro: A buried fire, discreet and not very sensitive to wind, that uses little wood and heats a pot well.
etapes: Dig a hole about 30 cm deep and 20 cm wide, keeping the turf aside.
On the wind side, dig a second hole 20 to 30 cm away, joined to the first by a slanting tunnel: this is the air intake.
Light the fire at the bottom of the main hole with tinder and kindling.
Put the pot directly over the opening, on two green sticks if needed.
When leaving: drown it, let it cool, fill in the holes and put the turf back.
attention: Don't do it among roots (they can smoulder) or on peaty ground.
Even buried, the fire is still subject to the local rules.
feu_dakota.source: US Army survival manual FM 3-05.70 (public domain), rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

reflecteur.intro: A wall behind the fire sends the heat back towards you or the shelter, and cuts the wind.
etapes: Drive in two pairs of stakes about 1 m behind the fire.
Stack logs between the stakes to form a wall 50 to 80 cm high.
Sit between the fire and the shelter: heat reaches you from both sides.
Without logs: a big dry rock or a tarp stretched at a safe distance.
attention: Never use wet or porous stones around the fire: the water they contain can make them burst.
reflecteur.source: US Army survival manual FM 3-05.70 (public domain), rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

arc_feu.intro: The most reliable friction method, but it takes practice and perfectly dry wood. Learn it at home, not on the day you need it.
etapes: Prepare the four parts: a board of soft, dry wood (lime, willow, poplar) about 2.5 cm thick; a straight, dry spindle about 2 × 25 cm, rounded at the top and flat at the bottom; a handhold (hollowed stone or hardwood) to hold the top of the spindle; a bow of flexible wood the length of your arm, with a taut cord.
Carve a small hollow in the board 2 cm from the edge, then cut a V-notch from the edge to the centre of the hollow.
Put the board on a piece of dry bark (which will catch the ember), your foot on the board.
Wrap the bow cord once around the spindle, put the spindle in the hollow, the handhold on top, wrist braced against your leg.
Start with long, slow strokes, then speed up, pressing harder and harder: black dust fills the notch and the smoke thickens.
Keep going a few seconds after the smoke appears, then remove the spindle: the dust should smoke on its own, that's the ember.
Slide it into a nest of very fine tinder, close the nest and blow gently until it flames.
attention: Dry dead wood gathered standing, never from the ground (too damp).
Blisters on the hands come quickly: protect your palm with a glove or cloth.
arc_feu.source: US Army survival manual FM 3-05.70 (public domain), rewritten and adapted for Bivaska

tissu_charbonne.intro: Two materials that catch a single spark and hold the ember for a long time. The cloth is prepared at home; tinder fungus grows in our forests.
etapes: Char cloth: cut squares of 100% cotton fabric (old T-shirt, jeans) a few centimetres across.
Lay them flat in a small closed metal tin with a small hole pierced in the lid.
Put the tin on a fire or stove: smoke comes out of the hole. Wait until it stops (5 to 10 minutes).
Remove it and let it cool without opening. The squares should be black and supple, not burnt. Keep them dry.
Tinder fungus: this hard, hoof-shaped fungus grows on dead beech and birch. Under the crust is a brown, felty layer.
Remove this felty layer, dry it well then beat it to soften it: it catches a fire steel's spark and holds an ember for many minutes.
attention: Only take tinder fungus from dead wood, in small quantities.
tissu_charbonne.source: US Army survival manual FM 3-05.70 (public domain), rewritten and adapted for Bivaska
